claims.text: Multi-component concentrated alloys in the proposed initial state are single-phase solid solutions.
These alloys contain inherent local chemical heterogeneities.
The proposed heat treatment promotes short-range chemical order.
Rapid quenching retains a comparatively near-random atomic distribution.
The degree of local chemical order alters the alloy's deformation-energy landscape.
Local chemical order introduces spatial energy fluctuations and localized hard atomic motifs.
Spatial variations in deformation energy increase dislocation pinning.
Increased dislocation pinning raises yield strength.
Enhanced local chemical order modifies work-hardening behavior relative to a near-random alloy.
Alloys with induced short-range order will exhibit significantly higher yield strength than the quenched baseline.
Alloys with induced short-range order will exhibit greater work-hardening rates than the quenched baseline.
Alloys with induced short-range order will show altered dislocation dynamics, including increased pinning and changes in dislocation density.
The comparison should use samples with identical bulk compositions and retained single-phase states.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold from room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures at moderate strain rates.
Extreme temperatures or strain rates may activate additional deformation mechanisms and invalidate the predicted trend.
No statistically significant difference in yield strength, work-hardening rate, or dislocation dynamics between ordered and baseline samples would falsify the hypothesis.
